I’m sixty-seven years old and I’ve farmed these seven mu in Quzhou County my whole life. I only finished primary school, so I don’t bother much with those government pamphlets, but I watch my neighbors closely and I remember what worked last year. This year I’m putting all seven mu into winter wheat and summer maize — the double crop. Everyone in the village does it, and at my age I don’t have the back for picking cotton by hand anymore. My son works in Shijiazhuang and only comes home for harvest, so I need crops that the combine can handle.

The wheat went in last October with the rotary tiller. I bought improved *jimai22* seed, about thirty jin per mu. At planting I spread one hundred-jin bag of compound fertilizer per mu — the one marked 18-22-5. Come green-up in spring, I’ll topdress with about thirty jin of urea if the wheat looks a little yellow. That works out to roughly sixteen kilograms of nitrogen per mu in total, which is what I’ve done for ten years and it hasn’t failed me. I’ll irrigate three times: once at green-up, once at jointing, and once at grain filling. Water costs money, but Lao Wang down the road skipped the third irrigation two years back and his yield dropped badly. I’ll spray four times too — herbicide once, insecticide twice, and fungicide once when the humidity rises. If the weather cooperates I should get about a thousand jin per mu, which is five hundred kilograms.

For the summer maize, I’ll sow hybrid *denghai605* straight after wheat harvest in early June. There’s no time to plough — we plant no-tillage right into the wheat stubble. I put down one eighty-jin bag of 28-6-6 compound fertilizer per mu, about eleven kilograms of nitrogen. I irrigate twice: once at sowing if it’s dry, and once at the trumpet stage. Four pesticide applications, same as the wheat. A normal year gives me about eleven hundred jin per mu, or five hundred and fifty kilograms.

I did think about planting two mu of cotton like my cousin, but cotton needs constant hand weeding and pruning. Wheat and maize are safer — the grain buyer drives to the village and pays cash on the spot.
